prompt: I'm the product manager at Northwind Clinics Software, and I need help deciding whether we should build a built-in appointment scheduling feature. Over the past three weeks I ran five customer calls with clinic office managers. Three of them brought up scheduling on their own. Two said they currently pay around $40 a month for a separate booking tool and would happily drop it. The other two never mentioned scheduling until I asked, and then said it would be nice to have. Our engineering lead estimates about 8 weeks of work for two developers. I'm assuming the clinics that mentioned it are representative of our 220 paying accounts, but honestly I'm not sure, because all five calls came from customers who had recently contacted support. I also don't know whether the clinics would actually switch away from their current booking tools, given that those tools hold their patient reminders. I'd like a short written recommendation I can bring to our leadership meeting on Thursday. It should say whether five calls is enough to commit, and if it isn't, what we should find out before deciding.

I'm a co-founder at Acme Ledger, a small bookkeeping app for freelancers, and we have capacity to build exactly one integration next quarter. Customers keep asking for three: a bank feed connection with a major regional bank, a sync with a popular invoicing tool, and a calendar integration for tracking billable time. In the last 90 days the bank feed came up in 34 support tickets, the invoicing sync in 21, and the calendar integration in 9. Most of the calendar requests, though, came from our highest-paying tier. Rough effort estimates are 6 weeks for the bank feed, 3 weeks for the invoicing sync, and 2 weeks for the calendar. I'm assuming the ticket counts reflect real demand and aren't just a handful of loud users. What I don't know is whether any of these requests are actually tied to people cancelling. I need a ranked recommendation with your reasoning that I can share with my co-founder Ravi and our two engineers before our planning session on October 28. It should also flag what evidence would change the order.

I run growth at Brightpath, a project management tool for small agencies. Our pricing page has become a recurring complaint. Over the last two months, 12 prospects on sales calls said the plans were confusing, and a few customers have written in asking what the difference is between our Team and Studio tiers. Our designer, Jane, wants to do a full redesign, which she estimates at about 4 weeks including copy and engineering. Pricing page visitors convert to trial at 3.1 percent. I don't have a good benchmark for that number. My assumption is that confusion on the page is costing us signups, but I can't tell whether these 12 people are a meaningful share of the roughly 1,800 monthly visitors or just the ones who happened to talk to sales. I also don't know if the confusion is about the page itself or about the tiers being badly designed in the first place. I'd like help deciding whether this complaint justifies a redesign right now. Please give me a brief I can send to Jane and our head of sales that explains what we should do next and why.

I'm a product manager at Fernhill Payroll. We're designing a new onboarding flow for small business owners setting up payroll for the first time. It only exists as a set of design mockups, and no customer has seen it. Today, about 45 percent of new signups abandon setup before running their first payroll. Most of them drop off at the step where they enter tax registration details. Our working assumption is that people abandon because the setup feels long and intimidating, not because they lack the information. That assumption is untested. One open question is whether we should talk to people who abandoned, people who finished, or both. I'm also unsure whether owners with an accountant behave differently from those without one. I have budget for about 8 interviews over the next three weeks, and our researcher Priya can help run them. I'd like a plan for these interviews covering who to recruit, what we're trying to learn, and roughly what we'd ask. It's for Priya and me to align on before recruiting starts on November 3.

I'm the founder of Tidewater Notes, a note-taking app for researchers. We just ran a survey of active users, and I'm not sure what to make of the results. We got 312 responses out of about 2,400 people we emailed. When asked how they would feel if they could no longer use the product, 24 percent said very disappointed, 48 percent said somewhat disappointed, and the rest said not disappointed. The very disappointed group skews heavily toward graduate students who use our citation feature. I'm assuming the people who responded are roughly representative of our active base, though they may lean toward our most engaged users. What I don't know is whether I should narrow our focus to the graduate student group or keep building for everyone. Our investors have asked for an update on product direction at our November board meeting. I need help interpreting what these numbers do and don't tell us, along with a written summary I can adapt for the board explaining what we'll do in response.

I lead product at Kestrel Analytics. I need help deciding whether to retire our custom report builder. Only 4 percent of our 610 accounts used it in the last 90 days. It accounts for a disproportionate share of bugs, and maintaining it takes about 20 percent of one engineer's time. The complication is Halvorsen Group, our largest customer at roughly 11 percent of annual revenue. Their finance team relies on the report builder every month, and their account manager says they've called it a key reason they renewed last year. Their renewal is in March 2027. I'm assuming most of the other 4 percent could move to our standard dashboards without much pain. I haven't checked that. I also don't know whether Halvorsen's needs could be met some other way, such as a scheduled export. I'd like a recommendation on what to do with this feature and how to handle Halvorsen. It's for our VP of Engineering and our head of customer success, who disagree on this. I'd like something we can discuss together next week.

I'm the product manager for Larkspur, an inventory app for independent retailers, and I own next quarter's discovery plan. I exported the last six months of support tickets, about 1,400 in total. Our support lead, Tomas, tagged them roughly. The biggest clusters were barcode scanning problems at around 280 tickets, confusion about stock transfers between locations at around 190, and requests for supplier ordering at around 150. A long tail covers everything else. I'm assuming support tickets are a reasonable signal of where customers struggle, but I know customers who quietly churn probably never file tickets. I also can't tell how many of the scanning tickets are actual bugs and how many are setup mistakes. We have one researcher and about 10 weeks. I'd like help turning this into a discovery plan for the quarter, covering what we should investigate, in what order, and what we'd hope to learn from each. It's for my manager and Tomas, and I need to present it at our quarterly kickoff on January 6.

I'm a co-founder of Oakmere Pet, which sells subscription pet food. We're considering a new product line of at-home health testing kits for dogs. A few customers have asked about it, about 15 emails over the past year. We also see that 30 percent of our 9,000 subscribers have bought our supplements. My co-founder Dana and I agree we don't want to write any code or sign a supplier contract until we have some evidence that people would actually pay for this. We're assuming a price around $79 per kit would be acceptable, but we have nothing to back that up. We also don't know whether demand would come mostly from existing subscribers or from new customers we'd have to acquire. We have about $5,000 and six weeks to find out. I'd like a plan for testing demand within that budget and timeline. It should spell out what result would tell us to go ahead and what would tell us to stop. Dana and I will use it to decide how to spend the next six weeks.

I'm the product manager at Corvid Travel, a booking tool for corporate travel managers. We built two clickable prototypes for a new trip approval screen. Version A shows approvals as a list. Version B groups them by traveler and shows the budget impact. Last week we ran a usability round with 6 travel managers, and each person tried both versions. Five of the six finished the main approval task in A. All six finished it in B, but B took noticeably longer for four of them. Two people said they preferred A because it felt faster. Three preferred B because of the budget view. One had no preference. I'm assuming these 6 participants are typical of our customers, though all of them came from mid-sized companies. I don't know how this would play out for managers approving 50 or more trips a week. Our designer, Mei, needs a decision by October 30 so engineering can start. I'd like help interpreting these results and choosing between the prototypes, or deciding if we need more testing first. Please write it up so I can share it with Mei and our engineering lead.

I'm the founder of Quillstone, and we're planning a scheduling assistant for independent tutors. Our team of three listed every assumption the idea depends on and came up with ten we haven't tested. They include: tutors spend more than 3 hours a week on scheduling, tutors would pay $15 a month, parents are willing to book through a link, tutors currently use a messy mix of texts and spreadsheets, tutors would switch from the free tools they use now, and we can reach tutors cheaply through online communities. The rest cover calendar sync, reminders, payment collection, and group sessions. We're assuming the problem is mainly about time rather than missed sessions, though we're not confident about that. We also don't know which assumption, if wrong, would sink the whole idea. We have about 4 weeks before we need to decide whether to commit to building. I'd like help figuring out which assumptions to test first and roughly how to test each one, ordered so our time goes furthest. This is for our team's planning meeting on Monday.
